::: {.note-meta}
Working note · version 0.1 · 27 November 2026 · follows [*Two Ways to Book the Wrong Room*](/notes/which-saturday/index.qmd) [· [PDF](what-the-grant-left-out.pdf)]{.content-visible when-format="html"}
:::

In [*Assuring one delegation*](/notes/delegation-assurance/index.qmd), I used a hypothetical flight booking. The assistant buys a non-refundable ticket for $640. It lands at noon. The written grant allows the purchase, and the assistant meets every condition in it.

Suppose you are checking the work. Put the grant beside the booking record, and the purchase complies. Now add the traveller’s original request. They had to arrive by 10 a.m.

The ticket still meets the grant. It also misses the deadline the traveller gave. With that extra record, you can identify a failure in how the job became a grant of authority: the hard arrival condition disappeared between the request and the instructions the assistant received. A check confined to those instructions would miss it.

That first example is a clean hypothetical—there is no argument about what “by 10 a.m.” meant, and we have the request, the omission, and the late arrival sitting right beside one another. Even there, though, catching the mismatch raises a practical problem. There is still a traveller who needs to get somewhere. If somebody spots the mistake while there is time to buy a replacement, who can authorize it? Who can pay for it? Finding the omission does not tell us who has another purchase within their authority or whose budget is available. I would want that route settled before handing over a non-refundable booking.

## Three ways a condition breaks

In a [later mock booking](/cases/index.qmd#grant-002), I could follow one condition all the way through. The traveller needed to land in Montréal by 9:30 p.m. on Thursday, but would take a nonstop landing by 10:30 p.m. The grant writer got that exception right in the record read back to the traveller. The traveller clarified two other points. When the writer then produced the final grant, the exception vanished from both the final record and the instructions the booking assistant received. I gave the assistant a nonstop landing at 10:15 p.m. It refused a flight the traveller had expressly allowed. Across the seven acceptable flights I tried, it refused two and sent five back to the traveller, because the same grant kept an earlier requirement to “present the selected flights … before purchasing,” even though the read-back record had said the assistant could buy without asking.

If I’d started my check with the final record and the grant, I’d have found them in agreement on the very point they’d both lost. Agreement between the two documents does not establish that either preserved the traveller’s terms.

Beside the noon ticket, the consequence runs the other way. Leaving out the hypothetical deadline lets a bad purchase through. Leaving out the observed exception takes a good option away. In both cases the traveller had already decided what was acceptable; the act of writing the grant changed which flights the assistant could choose.

I gave one outside reader, S.S., the traveller’s request and four flight offers, then the issued instructions. Reading the request, she found two flights acceptable, including the 10:15 p.m. nonstop, and wanted to ask the traveller which they preferred. Reading the instructions, she noticed, before I said anything, that the exception for a later nonstop was missing. After I reminded her of the two arrival times, she corrected which flight she meant and pointed only to the earlier connecting flight as eligible. When we traced the exchange, she pointed to the traveller’s follow-up, which restated the ordinary deadline and preference without mentioning the exception again. She didn’t say whether that silence withdrew it. Either way, the missing exception changed which flights she would put before the traveller—though it didn’t change her view that the traveller should be the one to choose.

The study’s key treats the exception as still standing. The traveller in these runs is scripted, and the key fixes their terms in advance. Had the record read back to them dropped the exception, the script would have restated it; the record had it right, so the reply didn’t mention it. A reader seeing the exchange without the script can fairly read that silence differently.

A condition doesn’t have to vanish to fail. In another set of mock runs, [three grant writers](/cases/index.qmd#grant-002) put the traveller’s 9:30 p.m. correction on the flight home instead of the flight out—the correction, as I scripted it, did not name which leg—so a reviewer checking only that the time appeared in the grant would have found it every time.

I [replayed those same three conversations](/cases/index.qmd#grant-003) from the point where the traveller corrected the record. With my original wording, five of the six new grants again put 9:30 on the flight home, and the sixth gave no arrival time at all. When I changed the traveller’s reply to “land in Montréal by 9:30 p.m. on Thursday the 12th,” all eight grants put the deadline on the outbound flight. Seven of the eight, however, also left the writer’s earlier deadline of 9 the next morning sitting right beside it. Three times, the booking assistant relied on that leftover morning time and permitted a flight landing at 12:15 a.m. Friday, even though the 9:30 p.m. deadline still ruled it out.

That makes three ways a condition can go wrong on its way into a grant:

* **It can be left out**, as the 10 a.m. deadline and the 10:30 p.m. exception were.
* **It can be put in the wrong place**, as the 9:30 p.m. deadline was.
* **It can be corrected while the version it replaced stays beside it**, as the 9 a.m. line did.

When the traveller corrects a condition, can the person using the grant tell which instruction the correction replaced?

Gotel and Finkelstein (1994) studied this problem in [*An Analysis of the Requirements Traceability Problem*](/reading.qmd#gotel-finkelstein): the difficulty of tracing a requirement back through the decisions made before it entered the specification. Here, that specification gives someone power to spend money. When the trail breaks before the grant is written, the error does not stay on paper. It governs which tickets get bought and which ones get turned down.

## What a typed record can and can’t fix

A natural answer is to stop asking a language model to read deadlines out of prose: put the limits into structured fields and let a mechanical checker apply them. That does not remove the problem; it moves it to the moment a phrase like “10:30” becomes a typed timestamp. If the typed record is going to govern the purchase, the read-back has to show the traveller the typed value (“arrive YUL by 22:30 Thu 12 Nov if nonstop”) rather than echoing their prose, and that record itself has to be the document that gets corrected.

I [tested that boundary against the archived final records](/cases/index.qmd#typed-check-001) from both studies, running a deterministic checker with no new API calls. I measured both the checker and the original prose reader, a language model from the archived runs, against the study’s key of what the traveller had asked for, across 812 flight decisions from 82 archived records—noting up front that 52 of those records are replays of 11 conversations, so they are not independent observations. It also isn’t a strict like-for-like comparison: the checker read each writer’s typed record, the prose reader read the written grant issued beside it, and the two documents went wrong in different places.

| Route | Agreed with the study key (of 812) | What drove the misses |
|:-----------|:-----|:------------------------------|
| **Typed checker (strict)** | 464 | Held flights back for the traveller whenever buy permission was missing from the record or a row broke the format (268 of the 271 cases where the prose reader matched and the checker didn’t). |
| **Typed checker (forgiving on format & buy permission)** | 719 | Avoided the reading errors found in the prose reader’s decisions, but still permitted **45 ruled-out flights** whose deadlines were mistyped in the record. |
| **Prose reader (a model, on the written grant)** | 717 | Made occasional reading errors, and permitted **all 45 of those ruled-out flights** too, plus four more. |

The gap on the strict run is revealing on its own: in the 44 replays scored for buy authority, the traveller’s go-ahead to buy without asking reached the prose grant 43 times, and the typed record only 5. Once I gave the checker the benefit of the doubt on buy permission and formatting, it avoided each of the reading errors I found in the prose reader’s decisions. It never misread an exception as a cap, never followed the leftover 9 a.m. line past 9:30 p.m., and never contradicted itself on the same typed time within one grant—whereas in two replays where “10:30” was typed as morning, the prose reader permitted one 10:15 p.m. nonstop and refused another with the exact same outbound.

What the checker could not fix was what had been mistyped into the record. All 45 ruled-out flights that the forgiving checker let through were also let through by the prose reader. Every one of them came from nine records tracing back to the three conversations where the 9:30 p.m. deadline landed on the flight home. Forty came from wrong deadlines written into both documents; five from a record with wrong deadlines paired with a prose grant that stated no deadlines at all.

So the forgiving checker and the prose reader finish two apart, 719 to 717, and the prose reader let through every one of the 45 ruled-out flights the checker allowed. A similar score doesn’t mean a safe purchase. Both routes carried the same wrong deadline, and only the traveller’s own words show it.

A typed check also fails safe only when it has a channel for what its fields don’t cover. Anything outside the schema (a routing preference like “not via Toronto,” an aisle seat, or an ambiguity the writer itself recorded as unresolved) needs explicit review rather than being dropped or silently guessed, and whatever remains uncertain goes to someone with authority to settle it. None of my mock intakes included an off-schema condition, yet one grant writer produced one anyway. It typed the nonstop exception as 10:30 p.m., then added a free-text note the format had no field for: whether 10:30 was a.m. or p.m. was “not clarified.” The written grant kept 10:30 p.m. and dropped the doubt. A checker built to kick unresolved items back returned seven flights the traveller would have accepted; the prose reader bought them. The traveller’s words did support evening, so the prose reader landed on the right outcome—but the grant silently erased a recorded doubt without showing whether it had been settled from the traveller’s words or still needed asking.

The same principle explains why an offset protocol defines its quantification method rather than leaving it to a verifier’s reading of a narrative: verification can be mechanical only where the quantities are defined. Once a question sits outside what the format captures, someone still has to check the underlying arrangement.

## When the earlier terms are unavailable

Before turning all of this into a practical check, it helps to see what the check can’t settle when the earlier terms are unavailable. Everything above depends on having the earlier terms in hand. A.P., a wedding planner I spoke with separately, pointed to earlier terms my repair café exercise never supplied.

In [*Two Ways to Book the Wrong Room*](/notes/which-saturday/index.qmd), Noor Haddad organizes the Tannery Row Repair Café. Her calendar has two Saturday sessions in Workshop B. Elliot, the venue coordinator, emails to say he is moving the café to the Garden Room for its next session. By the time Noor forwards the notice to her assistant, one Saturday has passed and another is ahead. Which booking did he mean?

A.P. asked a different question: what room had the venue promised Noor? He suggested checking any booking agreement to see whether it specified a room, then asking the venue about the change and what could be done.

The only agreement I supplied in the exercise was Noor’s grant to the assistant:

> The Delegatee may edit the room and source note of a session when the venue coordinator has confirmed the change for that session.

That sets the condition for changing a calendar entry. If confirmation for a specific session is unclear, the assistant must leave the entry alone and ask her. I supplied no venue booking agreement, and the calendar can’t tell a reviewer whether the venue had promised Workshop B, whether a substitution had already been agreed, or whether Noor still had a choice to make.

That matters because permission to record a room change is not permission to accept one. If Noor and the venue had already agreed on the Garden Room for an identified session, updating the calendar simply records that decision. If the venue had offered a substitute and Noor kept the decision, the assistant’s permission to edit the calendar would not give it that choice. I would want the grant to say which of those the assistant is doing.

This is where A.P.’s question marks the limit of the check. For the traveller, we have the earlier terms and can show what the grant dropped or misplaced. For Noor, A.P. identified an agreement a reviewer would need to see before concluding whether accepting the Garden Room was already agreed or still Noor’s to decide, and its absence from my exercise isn’t evidence that anything was left out. You can’t test a grant against terms nobody has established. Nor would finding the agreement, by itself, settle which Saturday Elliot meant.

## Testing a boundary before issuing the grant

Before issuing a grant, I would try one small check. It is a way of validating the grant in miniature before anyone relies on it: put the original request beside the draft grant and test a boundary rather than hunting for a word.

Take a flight the traveller would accept and one they would turn down. Does the grant draw the line in the same place, for the same reason? If a condition was relaxed or shifted, who had authority to agree? If a condition was corrected, can a reader tell what it replaced? What choice still belongs to the person who asked for the job? A grant can deliberately authorize fewer options than the requester would accept, or require approval on purpose. The test is whether a difference like that was the requester’s choice or crept in while the grant was being written.

The test’s first step, picking a flight the traveller would accept, can itself come out differently. A second reader, V.B., saw the instructions first, then the traveller’s request. Under the instructions, after one clarification, she settled on the earlier connecting flight; under the request, she called it the only flight meeting every requirement, ruling out the 10:15 p.m. nonstop by pointing to “before 8:30 would be nicer,” a line she had earlier described as flexible. Her replies don’t show whether the nonstop exception registered, and her review stopped before we looked at where the exception went. Afterward she wrote that the booking instructions didn’t exactly match the traveller’s and that an assistant should ask questions, while adding that she dislikes being “badgered by multiple Qs” once she has already said enough. S.S. had found that nonstop acceptable from the same request. Where two careful readers draw different lines, the person to ask is the traveller. That adds a further problem to what the grant dropped, about how a request gets understood in the first place, and I’ll come back to it in a later note.

::: {.content-visible when-format="typst"}
{{< pagebreak >}}
:::

Across the flight cases in this note, the check is short:

| Case (failure mode) | Test flight | What the draft grant does | Authority for the line |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Hypothetical flight** *(omitted deadline)* | Noon arrival (traveller would turn it down; asked to arrive by 10 a.m.) | Allows it; the 10 a.m. deadline is absent. | No traveller-authorized relaxation is recorded. That choice still belongs to the traveller. |
| **Observed run** *(omitted exception)* | 10:15 p.m. nonstop (traveller would accept it; allowed nonstops up to 10:30 p.m.) | Excludes it; the 10:30 p.m. nonstop exception is absent. | No traveller-authorized tightening is recorded. That choice still belongs to the traveller. |
| **Observed misplacement** *(deadline on wrong leg)* | Outbound landing after 9:30 p.m. Thursday, outside the nonstop exception (traveller would turn it down) | Allows it; the 9:30 p.m. deadline sits on the return flight instead—the error behind all 45 ruled-out flights above. | The traveller corrected the arrival deadline, not the flight home; the outbound limit was never lifted. |
| **Observed replay** *(replaced deadline left in)* | 12:15 a.m. Friday arrival (traveller would turn it down; corrected deadline to 9:30 p.m. Thursday) | Contains both 9:30 p.m. Thursday and the leftover 9 a.m. Friday line, with nothing marking which replaced which. | The traveller replaced the earlier deadline; the leftover 9 a.m. line carries no authority and should come out. |

I would hold any of those grants long enough to make the line clear—putting back what was dropped, moving a deadline back to the leg it governs, or removing an earlier limit a correction replaced. In the hypothetical case, if the available flights cannot meet the 10 a.m. deadline within the other conditions, the traveller needs the choice before a purchase commits them. A person authorized to approve extra spending may also be needed. Permission to spend more does not, on its own, settle whether arriving late is acceptable.

That is a small enough check to use on an ordinary booking. Take an outcome the requester would accept and one they would turn down, and test whether the grant draws the line in the same place, for the same reason, or returns the choice to someone entitled to make it. One pair checks one boundary, not the whole grant, so repeat it for each condition that matters and for combinations that matter, such as the deadline and the nonstop exception. Keep the whole exchange with the grant—the request and every reply that changed it—so the next person checking the work can run the same test. For a traveller, it is the difference between checking that the assistant followed the grant and noticing that it bought a ticket too late or refused a flight they had already allowed.
